g.text: Cancel is the hot path - which is what kills the heap
In real markets most orders are CANCELLED, not filled. Any structure with O(n) cancel is disqualified however fast its matching.
FIFO: oldest matches first -> time priority
FIFO: oldest matches first -> time priority
FIFO: oldest matches first -> time priority
The price level, then a FIFO queue within it, IS price-time priority - encoded as the SHAPE of the data rather than as
comparator logic, so a bug cannot violate the fairness rule.
Given an id you get the object; the object holds prev/next, so
unlinking it from its FIFO queue is a constant-time pointer update.
NO SEARCH OF ANY KIND. This is the heap's fatal flaw solved.
Intrusive means links live INSIDE Order - one allocation, and the
data plus its links share a cache line. Doubly-linked means
unlinking needs no predecessor search; singly-linked would make
cancel O(n) again, which is exactly the mistake to avoid.
best price O(1) at the head,
but insert is O(n) and cancel
requires a scan. Dead on arrival.
but CANCEL BY ID IS O(n), and it
O(1) best, O(log n) on distinct
prices are integers in fixed ticks,
so the price IS an array index.
Used by the fastest real engines.
Which resting order matches first - and the market-design consequence
rewards SPEED. Encourages tight spreads and, unavoidably, a latency arms race.
best price, then proportionally by SIZE
rewards posting size. Reduces the arms race; encourages inflated order sizes.
best price, then larger, then time
collect over an interval, cross at one price
Price-time is the equities standard AND the one the data structure expresses natively - the FIFO queue at each price level IS
time priority. Pro-rata would require walking every order at a level and computing allocations: O(orders at level), not O(1).
The honest observation: price-time CREATES the latency arms race that makes this entire design necessary. If matching were a
periodic batch auction, tens-of-microseconds latency would be pointless and the whole one-box architecture unjustified. The
design's most extreme constraint is downstream of a market-design decision - which is a good thing to be able to see.
